title: Weekly: mid-task model switching, an agent runtime at the CNCF, an AWS emulator written by agents, harnesses that change whether a model follows the rules, coding agents that keep going after a correct patch, harm before the model sees the input, and a monthly statement for every AI agent
summary: Weekly Digest for Oct 30–Nov 12, 2026: unsponsored New Stack coverage of Google's claim that switching models mid-task cuts quota and time, Nvidia's donation of the OpenShell agent runtime to the CNCF, and an AWS emulator that AWS says agents wrote and will maintain. Four arXiv cs.AI papers measure how a harness changes a fixed model's compliance with banking conduct rules, how often coding agents keep working after their first correct patch, how untrusted files can do harm before any content reaches the model, and how transcript-reading judges miss forbidden writes. Our proof of concept of the week is a monthly agent statement: a plain-language, one-page-per-agent record of what each AI agent did, what it cost, and who approved it.

sections.heading: The New Stack — mid-task routing, a donated agent runtime, and an emulator agents maintain
bullets: "Google's Gemini 4 coding agent now switches models mid-task — and finishes 19% faster," Amanda Caswell, The New Stack, Nov 12, 2026. Caswell reports that Google is pairing the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen with the more capable Gemini 4 Carbon and switching between them mid-task through Orchestrator, a new feature in its Antigravity development environment, rather than running the stronger model for the whole session. Google's own claim: the pairing gets nearly the same results as Carbon alone while using 24% less quota and finishing tasks 19% faster. Caswell notes that Google's benchmark citations don't match (the main Gemini announcement cites Terminal-Bench 4.0, the Antigravity announcement 4.1), and that Google hasn't published Carbon's standalone success rate, a per-task breakdown, or how Orchestrator decides when to switch and what those handoffs cost in extra tokens and latency. Orchestrator is limited to Google AI Ultra subscribers for now.

"Why Nvidia gave OpenShell to the CNCF," Frederic Lardinois, The New Stack, Nov 11, 2026. Nvidia's Ali Golshan, who leads the project, tells The New Stack that securing and governing AI agents is an infrastructure job for the same platform teams that already run Kubernetes, which is why Nvidia donated OpenShell, a runtime that sandboxes an agent and enforces policy on the files, networks, credentials, and model endpoints it can reach, to the CNCF as a Sandbox project. The Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation was another possible home. Per the article, Nvidia launched OpenShell at GTC in March 2026, the CNCF formally accepted it in late September, and the project dropped its alpha label with its 0.1.0 release in September. The article says the CNCF project page lists about 380 contributing organizations; Golshan says about 50 to 60 companies have built on it so far, and that an independent security committee is still being worked out.

"AWS had its agents build a free and open emulator for AWS. They now maintain it, too." Frederic Lardinois, The New Stack, Nov 11, 2026. AWS launched AWS Emulator, a local, offline emulator that lets developers and coding agents test against AWS APIs without handing agents AWS credentials. AWS says agents wrote the code and will keep maintaining it, with human engineers fixing the agent system rather than editing the emulator by hand. Per AWS via The New Stack: it supports 438 public AWS API models covering more than 200 services, is written in Rust, carries a Creative Commons Zero license because AWS wasn't sure it could copyright the agents' work, and AWS will take issues but not pull requests. AWS's Tom Callaway says the emulator was built for testing coverage, not to reproduce what the real services compute. He expects new services to be supported within "days, not weeks," though the team hasn't yet seen how that plays out in public.

sections.heading: arXiv cs.AI — curated recent
bullets: "The Harness Is the Model: Agent Scaffolding Changes a Fixed LLM's Compliance with Banking Conduct Rules, Unevenly Across Models" (arXiv:2611.06116), Mehmet Murat Huyut, submitted Nov 4, 2026. Thesis: banks validate models but put a model into production inside a harness, and that harness can change compliance with conduct rules even when the model is held fixed. Per the abstract: four open-weight models each ran five harnesses on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank (3,120 two-turn episodes scored from the executed tool trace). Pooled across models, the harness moved the correct-case rate only between 87.3% and 92.1%. For one model, though, the gap between its best and worst harness was 11.5 percentage points, enough to move it from first to last of the four, while for another the harness made no detectable difference; the author calls the overall model-by-harness interaction suggestive rather than conclusive. A same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals, rules that require date arithmetic failed in every harness, and in an exploratory analysis 26% of violations came with a customer message denying the action the agent had just executed.

"Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late" (arXiv:2611.14960), Musa Cim, Burak Topcu, and Mahmut Taylan Kandemir, submitted Nov 11, 2026. Thesis: coding agents often reach a correct patch well before they stop, so judging only the final result hides extra work and the occasional undoing of a correct fix. Per the abstract: across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets, 38–82% of successful runs reached a correct solution on their first source-code edit. Yet in successful runs on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual, steps after the solution made up a median of 35–37% of the run for Qwen3-Coder and 54–60% for Laguna-XS.2, mostly spent verifying and exploring the repository. In 1–8% of cases the continued activity undid the earlier correct patch and left the final solution incorrect.

"Step-Zero Attack: Agent Safety Before Observability" (arXiv:2611.01953), Tian Qin, Yuhang Jiang, Junzhe Chen, Lit Sin Tan, and Lijie Wen, submitted Nov 1, 2026. Thesis: some harm happens during the first processing of an untrusted archive, network response, or image, before any of that content reaches the model, so defenses that only inspect what the model reads come too late. Per the abstract: across seven harnesses and six models, each agent received only a path or URL to a crafted input, paired with a harmless twin showing the same visible fields. 32 of 42 harness-model pairs overran a 4 MiB disk budget, 26 of 42 before the model saw any of the archive's contents, and four of the six models did so in every round (84 of 84), while every twin stayed within budget. The authors report that a gate counting the bytes each call produces kept every routed extraction within budget while agents completed 25 of 28 tasks. For network and image inputs, the abstract says the risk shifts to what the agent writes to disk.

"When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench" (arXiv:2611.14581), Sungbin Im, submitted Nov 10, 2026. Thesis: scoring a finished database state against a gold answer and asking an LLM judge to read the transcript are not interchangeable, and a transcript-only review can miss writes that should never have happened. Per the abstract: in 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains, the judge repeated its own verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring only 56.2% of the time. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write; the judge passed 10 to 11 of them with or without the policy or transcript, and a stronger judge still passed 6, while a rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred caught all 11 without calling a model. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates, and the study's verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The author points to a candidate cause in the traces: the gates' evidence summary dropped order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected.

sections.heading: Proof of concept of the week — a monthly statement for every AI agent
bullets: The problem: this week several vendors announced agent-governance platforms with features such as spend caps, audit records and human approval of fixes, so those controls are quickly becoming standard. But a 60–90 person company running agents across several SaaS tools often has no platform team, and at month end it still can't easily answer three questions: what did our agents do, what did it cost, and who approved it?

The idea: a plain-language Monthly Agent Statement, one page per agent, that reads like a bank statement. It shows what the agent touched, what it spent, which actions a person approved, and what changed since last month. It completes a series: the agent register says which agents you have, the permission slip says what they may do, and the statement shows what they did and what it cost.

Where this week's launches leave a gap: by their own announcements, Mirantis's Agent Platform is aimed at platform engineering, SRE and IT operations teams running agents on Kubernetes; IBM and Microsoft's Imagine Enterprise is aimed especially at regulated industries and comes with hands-on engineering support from both companies for qualifying engagements; and Expedient's AI CTRL runs each client in a dedicated instance in Expedient's own cloud. None of the three is pitched at a small business whose agents are spread across everyday SaaS tools.

Honest limits: self-hosting is not the same as keeping data local. Per The Next Web, Anthropic's new self-hosted Claude Managed Agents keeps agent histories and credentials on the customer's systems, but each model call still goes to an outside provider, and some features, such as webhooks and scheduled runs, are missing. A statement can record where data went but can't change it. It looks backward, so it won't stop a bad action as it happens; costs from tools that don't share usage data stay estimates; and it's a plain-language record, not a security audit or a compliance certification.

sections.heading: What operators should take from this cluster
bullets: Validate the model-harness pair, not the model alone, and score from the action or tool log rather than the conversation, which can deny an action the agent already took.
Treat a correct mid-run patch as a signal to stop or snapshot; leaving the agent running can take up a large share of the run and, in a small share of runs, undo the good patch.
Put resource and write limits on the processing step itself, not only on what reaches the model, and count bytes and destinations before unpacking or storing untrusted input.
Don't treat an LLM judge's transcript verdict as proof that a write was allowed; in one study, a cheap expected-versus-occurred check caught forbidden writes the judges missed.

Treat mid-task routing speedups as vendor claims until the routing policy and the stronger model's standalone rate are published. When the alternative is handing credentials to a coding agent, prefer a local emulator or a sandboxed agent runtime you can inspect.

bottomLine: This week, treat the harness as part of the system you validate, stop or snapshot coding agents when they first produce a correct change, and put limits on processing and writes rather than relying on the model's account of what it did. Take vendor speed and quota figures as claims until the comparison is fully specified, and keep agent tests and policy enforcement in infrastructure you control. For a small team, a monthly statement of what each agent did, what it cost, and who approved it is a simple place to start.
